buckingmill-handbook-assembly-text: Place the frame where the whole machine has room: it is six blocks long, three wide and four high, and runs away from you, with the block you place as the middle of its near end. The far end takes the axle and the trunks; the logs come out of the near end. Then fit Immersive Woodworking's sawmill parts with rightmouse, in any order: two saw sashes, a crankshaft, feed levers and a blade kit, which puts a blade in each saw, so it goes in after both sashes. No carriage is needed. The crankshaft strokes the two saws back and forth across the trunk, and they sink through it under their own weight. When they reach the bottom they trip the levers, which engage a windlass that winds them back up on ropes; at the top the carriage trips the levers back, the windlass lets go, and they start down again. While it is turning the mill never stops: with no trunk on the bed the saws keep going up and down. ctrl + rightmouse takes the blade kit back out. The other parts come back only when you break the frame, which drops every fitted part. In creative mode, ctrl + rightmouse on an unassembled mill fits its next part, as on the woodworking stations, with nothing taken from you.
buckingmill-handbook-power-text: Connect a turning axle to the far end of the mill, high up, where the shaft ends (the top of the end, in the middle). The assembled mill is a heavy load, twice a plank sawmill's, and it only cuts while its shaft turns at a fair speed. Until it is assembled it barely loads the shaft.
buckingmill-handbook-trunks-text: The mill cuts Logging Expanded tree trunks of any size, one at a time. Trunks must have their branches removed first while Logging Expanded asks for that. On the bed every one-block-thick trunk looks the same, four blocks long, and every two-block-thick one five blocks long, whatever its own length; the trunk you take back out is the one you loaded. Carry a trunk on your shoulder and hold rightmouse on the mill to load it. It goes on when the saws are at the top of their cycle: if they are not, keep the button held and it goes on as they come up. A trunk storage rack feeds the running mill. Stand it on the ground right against the mill's far end, under the axle, at the level of the block you placed the mill on: one of its two blocks must be in one of the three blocks just beyond that end, and it may run either way, in line with the bed or across it. The mill takes the rack's top trunk whenever the bed is empty and the saws come round to the top. A branched trunk on top of the rack holds the line until you deal with it. The mill's info says what the rack offers, or why nothing is coming. With no rack or rosser there ready, the mill takes a trunk lying on the ground in those three blocks, its middle in one of them, the same way. A rosser feeds the mill as a rack does: place the rosser on the block just beyond the mill's far end, in line with its middle, looking the way you looked when you placed the mill. The mill takes each debarked trunk off it when the bed is empty and the saws come to the top, and a debarked trunk gives debarked logs. ctrl + rightmouse takes the trunk back out onto your shoulder, but only before a quarter of it is cut.
buckingmill-handbook-yield-text:
Every log stored in a trunk takes 8 turns of the shaft with copper blades, and gives 2 logs of its wood, which slide off the rails at the near end. A cut trunk's resin and branches are lost, as on a sawhorse.

After each cut the saws wind back up to the top, which takes 6 turns of the shaft from the bottom; with no trunk they take another 6 to come down, so an empty cycle is 12 turns. A trunk taken back out early lets them carry on down from where they are. The next trunk can only go on while they are at the top.

Better blades cut faster, by their metal's tool tier: bronze about 1.35 times as fast as copper, iron 1.7 times and steel about twice (gold and silver no faster than copper). Only the cut is faster; the saws go up and down empty at the same speed whatever the blades.

The blade kit loses 1 durability for every log stored in a cut trunk. A worn out kit breaks and the mill stops, its saws where they are, until a new one is fitted.

A mill that stops turning leaves its saws where they are. While it is stopped, hold <hk>rightmouse</hk> on it with an empty hand to wind them up to the top by hand; a trunk on the bed stays, and when the mill turns again the saws come back down onto it where the cut had got to. These figures are the defaults of BuckingSawmillSettings in ModConfig/seraphhorizons.json.
blockdesc-rosser-frame-*: The frame of a mechanically powered ring debarker that draws Logging Expanded tree trunks through a spinning ring of scrapers, stripping their branches and bark. Fit a sawmill crankshaft, four large gear sections for the ring, two hoops for its tyres, four rods for the feed rolls, two metal plates for the limb breaker, sawmill feed levers and four bark spud heads of one metal to assemble it.
rosser-error-needs-ring: The tyres and the scraper heads go on the ring. Fit the four ring sections first.
rosser-error-wrong-metal: The rosser's hoops, rods and plates must be iron, meteoric iron or steel.
rosser-error-needs-full-set: The scraper heads go on as a set: hold four bark spud heads of one metal.

rosser-handbook-assembly-text: Place the frame where the whole machine has room: it is sixteen blocks long, five wide and four high, and runs away from you, with the block you place as the middle of its near end. Trunks go in at the far end and come out debarked at the near end. Then fit its parts with rightmouse, in any order, except that the tyres and the scraper heads go on the ring: a sawmill crankshaft for the drive, four large gear sections for the toothed ring, two hoops for its tyres, four rods for the infeed and outfeed rolls, two metal plates for the limb breaker, sawmill feed levers for the treadle and the feed's levers, and four bark spud heads of one metal for the scraper tips. Hoops, rods and plates must be iron, meteoric iron or steel, as the woodworking machines' parts are; the heads may be any metal. A click fits as many as the part still needs from the stack in your hand, and four rods fill both sets of rolls. With no trunk in it, ctrl + rightmouse takes unused heads back out. The other parts come back only when you break the frame, which drops every fitted part (the heads only if unused) and the trunk. In creative mode, ctrl + rightmouse on an unassembled rosser fits its next part, as on the woodworking stations, with nothing taken from you.
rosser-handbook-power-text:
Connect a turning axle to the rosser's right-hand side as you look along it from its near end: to the top block of that side, ten blocks back from the near end, beside the ring. It may turn either way. The assembled rosser is a heavy load, and it only feeds while its shaft turns at a fair speed; the ring spins whenever the shaft turns.

Water is optional. A Pipes and Power Expanded water pipe against the other side, on the third block up, nine blocks back from the near end, fills a small reservoir that drips onto the trunk just ahead of the ring. A full reservoir wets ten logs. Each wet log gives half as many pieces of bark again, and the special kinds of bark more often.
rosser-handbook-trunks-text: The rosser takes Logging Expanded tree trunks of any size, branched or not, one at a time. On the beds every one-block-thick trunk looks the same, four blocks long, and every two-block-thick one five blocks long, whatever its own length. It does not take trunks that are already debarked. Carry a trunk on your shoulder and hold rightmouse on the rosser to load it. It goes onto the infeed bed at the far end, and its weight on the treadle starts the feed as soon as the shaft turns. The rolls draw it through the limb breaker, which snaps off its branches, and the spinning ring, whose scrapers take off its bark, onto the outfeed bed. A trunk storage rack feeds the running rosser its top trunk whenever it is empty. Stand it on the ground right against the far end: one of its two blocks must be in one of the three blocks just beyond that end. A debarked trunk on top of the rack holds the line until you take it off. With no rack there ready, the rosser takes a trunk lying on the ground in those three blocks, its middle in one of them, the same way. A rack stood the same way against the near end takes each debarked trunk while it has room for it; a full one leaves the trunk on the bed until there is room. A bucking sawmill takes the debarked trunk straight onto its bed when its saws come to the top. Place the mill first, then place the rosser on the block just beyond the mill's far end, in line with its middle, looking the same way. Otherwise the trunk waits on the outfeed bed. ctrl + rightmouse takes the trunk back onto your shoulder while it waits on either bed, but not while it is in the rolls.
rosser-handbook-yield-text:
Branches come off as sticks, one for every two branches, at the chute on the side away from the axle, as the trunk goes through the limb breaker. Bark comes off at the ring, log by log: Immersive Woodworking's bark for the trunk's wood, as a bark spud gives it. With water, each log's bark is half as much again and the better kinds are more likely.

The feed is geared, so every thin trunk goes through at one speed and every thick one at a slower one: with copper heads a thin trunk takes about 68 turns of the shaft and a thick one about 169. Better heads feed faster, by their metal's tool tier: bronze about 1.35 times as fast as copper, iron 1.7 times and steel about twice.

The four heads together last four times as long as a bark spud of their metal, losing one point for every log stored in a debarked trunk. Worn out heads break and the rosser stops until new ones are fitted. These figures are the defaults of RosserSettings in ModConfig/seraphhorizons.json.
machineoil-info-dry: Dry: it takes {0}× the power to turn. Pour oil on it.
machineoil-text: The heavy machines need oil: the helve hammer, the pulverizer, the automated sawmill, the powered chopper, the bucking sawmill and the rosser. The quern, axles, gears and the other transmission parts do not. Dry A machine is built dry, and runs dry again once its oil is used up. A dry machine works as well as an oiled one, but it takes three times the power to turn: on a windmill or water wheel that is already working hard, it can slow the whole network or stall it. It smokes while it turns. Any oil at all in the tank, however little, and it turns as easily as ever. Oiling Hold a bucket, jug or bowl of oil and press rightmouse on any part of the machine: as much as fits goes in, and the rest stays in the container. Holding oil, the click always pours, whatever else it would have done there. Lumps of rendered fat go in the same way, half a litre each. The oils: flax and olive oil, every Expanded Foods cooking oil (seed, nut, olive, rice bran and the rest), and lard, liquid or hardened. Oil cannot be taken back out, and breaking the machine loses it. How long it lasts The tank holds 1000 points, 100 to the litre: one full bucket. Only work uses oil, never turning idle: a helve hammer a tenth of a point for each strike on an anvil with work on it, a pulverizer half a point an item, the sawmill 2 points a log, the chopper 1 point a log, and the bucking sawmill and the rosser 2 points for each log stored in a trunk. A full tank lasts days of steady work. Look at the machine to see how much is left.

woodworking-overview-text: Wood leaves the forest as tree trunks. You turn them into logs, boards, support beams, firewood and bark at a few stations, each built in the world. The chapters below follow them in the order you will need them. 1. Trunks A felled tree leaves one tree trunk on the ground holding all its logs. Drag it where you need it, or carry it on your shoulder to a station. Cut its branches off with a knife. An axe or a saw gets wood out of a trunk on the ground, but wastefully: an axe gives one log for every two the trunk holds. 2. Sawhorses A primitive sawhorse, built from sticks and rope, takes every log out of a trunk, and saws logs into boards or support beams. Standard and advanced sawhorses saw more boards per log. 3. Splitting block Right-click an upright log with an axe to make a splitting block. Chop logs on it into firewood, and firewood into sticks. Upgraded with iron, it gives more firewood per log. 4. Bark Debarking logs on a sawhorse, or debarking a splitting block, gives bark: tanning bark for tannin, birch bark for tar, bast for rope, medicinal bark for poultices. 5. Machines With mechanical power, an automated sawmill saws logs and an automated chopper splits them for you.
woodworking-trunks-text: Felling A felled tree leaves a tree trunk lying on the ground rather than loose logs. The trunk holds every log of the tree and, until you cut them off, its branches. Pine and acacia trunks also hold resin. A trunk fits in no bag or chest: work it where it lies, or move it. Moving a trunk Hold rightmouse on a trunk with an empty hand to drag it after you, and let go to leave it. The more logs it holds, the heavier it is and the slower it follows. Tie a rope to it to tow it behind an animal or a cart, or to tie it to a post. Walking into a trunk shoves it, and trunks float. To load a station, shoulder the trunk with shift + rightmouse and an empty hand. You walk very slowly while you carry it, slower the more logs it holds. Hold rightmouse on a sawhorse, a storage or heating rack, a rosser or a bucking sawmill to load it, or on a cart's or sled's storage to stow it. Put it down on the ground as you put down anything you carry. A trunk you take back off any of them goes onto your shoulder. Debranching Hold rightmouse on a branchy trunk with a knife. Each 2-second hold cuts off up to 12 branches and gives a stick for each. A trunk with branches left can't be worked with an axe or a saw, or loaded on a sawhorse. With shears instead, a hold turns 12 branches into a sapling. Working a trunk on the ground Hold rightmouse with an axe to take off one log for every two the trunk holds, or with a saw to cut 6 boards per log. With a hammer in your offhand, the axe gives debarked logs at the same rate, but no bark. A bark spud held on a trunk with no branches debarks the whole trunk in one long hold, half a second per log, and drops each log's bark. Working a trunk on the ground wastes wood: load it on a sawhorse as soon as you can. Storage and resin A trunk storage rack holds 4 trunks. A trunk heating rack over a fire drains the resin from pine and acacia trunks. A stick storage holds up to 128 sticks. Their pages say how to build them. Next: Sawhorses. Back to Woodworking.
woodworking-sawhorses-text: Sawhorses take logs out of trunks and saw them into boards and support beams. There are three, each better than the last, all built in the world. Primitive sawhorse Put exactly 18 sticks in a pile on the ground and right-click the pile with a knife: it becomes a large stick frame. Hold rightmouse on the frame with 4 rope to finish the sawhorse. Standard sawhorse Put exactly 36 boards of one wood in a pile and right-click it with a hammer to make a board frame. Add 2 debarked logs, then hold rightmouse with 20 copper or bronze nails and strips in your hand and a hammer in your offhand. The sawhorse is of the boards' wood and the nails' metal. Advanced sawhorse Make a board frame and add 2 debarked logs, as above. Then add 2 iron plates and 4 iron rods, and hold rightmouse with 20 iron nails and strips and a hammer in your offhand to finish the advanced sawhorse. Loading Carry a debranched trunk to a sawhorse on your shoulder and hold rightmouse on it to load the trunk (see Trunks), or right-click it with up to 16 logs of one wood. Right-click a loaded sawhorse with empty hands to take the load back: a trunk onto your shoulder, logs into your inventory. A sawhorse takes only logs with their bark on. Working Each hold of rightmouse, under a second, works one log and costs the tool 1 durability: • An axe takes off a log. • A saw cuts boards: 9 per log on the primitive sawhorse, 12 on the standard, 18 on the advanced. • A saw with shift held cuts support beams: 2 per log on the primitive and standard sawhorse, 3 on the advanced. • A bark spud, or an axe with a hammer in your offhand, gives a debarked log and drops that log's bark. From a trunk, the advanced sawhorse works 2 logs per hold with an axe, with or without a hammer, and with a bark spud, and gives 3 logs for them: the axe still loses 1 durability, a bark spud 2. Breaking a sawhorse drops its load and gives back about three quarters of what it took to build. Next: Splitting block. Back to Woodworking.
woodworking-splittingblock-text: Making one Place a log upright and right-click it with an axe: the log becomes a splitting block of its wood, for 1 durability. There is no crafting recipe. Breaking a splitting block gives it back, with its wood and upgrades. Chopping Put a log on the block with rightmouse, then hold rightmouse with an axe: • a log splits into 2 half-logs; • put a half-log back and it splits into 3 firewood, or 4 on an advanced block; • firewood goes on the block too, and splits into 2 sticks. So a log gives 6 firewood, or 8 on an advanced block. A maul splits a whole log into firewood in one pass, at the same yield. Debarked logs split the same way; quarter logs split straight into firewood. Take wood back off the block with ctrl + rightmouse. shift + rightmouse with an axe leaves the axe stuck in the block until you take it back the same way. Upgrades Upgrade an empty block, without shift or ctrl, in this order: 1. Debarked: hold rightmouse with a bark spud, or with an axe and a hammer in your offhand, as long as stripping a log takes. The block's bark drops on top. 2. Bound: right-click with 2 iron hoops. 3. Advanced: hold rightmouse for 3 seconds with 8 iron nails and strips and a hammer in your offhand. Debarked and bound blocks chop like a new one, 6 firewood per log. The advanced block gives 8, and only an advanced block can be the bed of an automated chopper. Next: Bark. Back to Woodworking.
woodworking-bark-text: Getting bark Bark comes off logs in three places: • on a sawhorse, debarking with a bark spud or an axe with a hammer in your offhand: bark for every log debarked; • on a splitting block, when you debark the block itself: bark for one log; • on a trunk on the ground, with a bark spud, which debarks the whole trunk at once: bark for every log it holds. An axe with a hammer in your offhand on a trunk on the ground gives debarked logs, but no bark. Which bark Each debarked log gives 3 pieces of one kind of bark, chosen by chance from its wood; otherwise it is ordinary bark. A log's handbook page lists the chances under "When stripped". Oak, acacia and larch are good for tanning bark, birch for birch bark, bald cypress and redwood for bast, kapok and ebony for medicinal bark. A bark spud finds the special kinds more often than an axe and hammer, and a spud of better metal more often still. Uses • Tanning bark: soak it in a barrel of water for weak tannin, or in weak tannin for strong tannin. Dried bark soaks faster, and crushed bark (dried bark ground on a quern) faster still. • Birch bark: pack it into a perforated pot set on an empty clay pot, seal it with clay and fire it in a pit kiln for birch tar, which stands in for resin. • Bast: 6 make a rope on the crafting grid. It also makes poultices. • Medicinal bark: simmer it in a pot with water for bark decoction, for healing poultices. • Ordinary bark: fuel for a pit kiln in place of sticks, and compost in a barrel. Next: Machines. Back to Woodworking.
woodworking-machines-text: Both machines run on mechanical power: connect an axle from a windmill or water wheel. Each is a frame you craft (it needs support beams; its page shows the recipe), place, and complete by installing its parts with rightmouse, in any order. Only the blade kit or the head can be taken back out, with ctrl + rightmouse; break the frame to recover the other parts. Automated sawmill Install a carriage, a saw sash, a crankshaft and feed levers, then a blade kit in the sash. Feed it logs or debarked logs, by hand or through a chute. By default a log comes out as 24 boards and a debarked log as 6 support beams; shift + rightmouse on the frame switches to boards only or beams only. Automated chopper Install a drive, an arm and an advanced splitting block as the bed, then a chopper head in the arm. A splitting block that is not advanced is refused, so upgrade it first. Load it with logs or firewood, by hand or through a chute. A log comes out as 8 firewood in one pass, and firewood as sticks. Breaking the frame gives the advanced splitting block back. Back to Woodworking.

gearreclamation-text: The rusty gears found in ruins are salvage: nothing is built from one. A machine that wants a gear wants a steel gear, and the old gears can be reclaimed into them, a batch at a time, in four steps. Only one gear in ten comes out sound; the rest are scrap, steel bits for the furnace. 1. Boil Boil the gears in a cooking pot over a fire with lye: Oils Resoaped's lye, or Expanded Matter's caustic soda or washing soda. A quarter litre for every gear, the gears in one, two or three slots of the pot, the same number in each; four gears take a litre. They come out degreased, the old grease gone so the acid reaches the rust evenly. 2. Pickle Pickle the degreased gears in acid in a pickling tub until the rust is gone. They come out pickled: bare metal. 3. Neutralize Seal the pickled gears in a barrel with lime water, a tenth of a litre a gear, for 2 hours. They come out neutralized. 4. Oil Seal the neutralized gears in a barrel with lard, a tenth of a litre a gear (or hardened lard, a fifth), for 4 hours. They come out oiled. The moment you take oiled gears, each one is decided: one in ten is a steel gear, and each of the rest is a steel bit. Flash rust Bare metal rusts fast. Pickled and neutralized gears stay bare for 8 hours, and over the next 2 they rust back into rusty gears, the whole batch's work lost. Keep moving: pickle, neutralize and oil without a long wait between.

picklingtub-handbook-text: The tub holds one liquid and one batch of up to 8 gears. Pour the liquid in with a bucket or jug, right-click with gears to add them, and right-click with an empty hand to take the batch out. An empty bucket takes the liquid back out. A batch uses up a litre of the liquid when it is done; taken out early, it gives the gears back unchanged and the litre goes back into the tub. Adding gears to a running batch starts it again. Pickling. Degreased gears go into dilute acid, one part acid to ten of water, until the metal looks grey and clean: vinegar takes about a day, sulfuric acid about 8 hours, hydrochloric acid about 2. Then take them out: past a grace of half the pickling time the acid starts on the steel and eats the batch to steel bits, one gear at a time, quickest in the strongest acid. Check on it every few minutes. A steel gear dipped in acid for a quarter of that time comes out bare. Brine. Steel gears left in brine rust through into rusty gears in about 2 days; bare ones, fresh from the acid, in about 4 hours. About one in ten over-rusts to steel bits. Large gears are not rusted.

steelbits-error-few: Each ingot's place takes {0} steel bits
steelbits-handbook-text: Steel bits melt at 1502 °C, hotter than any fuel burns (coke reaches 1340 °C), so no forge or crucible melts them. Two ways take them back into steel. Cementation furnace In a stone coffin, 20 steel bits take the place of one iron ingot. Hold at least 20 and press shift + rightmouse on the coffin where an ingot would go: 20 bits go in, packed as one. A full coffin holds 16 such places, 320 bits, between its 5 layers of coke or charcoal, and is fired as for iron; it gives 16 blister steel ingots. Bits and iron ingots cannot share a coffin. Bits can also be packed beforehand, 20 at a time in the crafting grid, into packed steel bits, which go in the same way. Bessemer converter Steelmaking Expanded's Bessemer converter takes steel bits as cold scrap: holding them, press rightmouse on the vessel's upper hatch to charge them in with a raw iron charge, before the blow. Each bit is 5 units of steel, a twentieth of an ingot, and comes out as steel with the rest of the heat; each also cools the bath by 4 °C, which harder blast buys back.

Or smith one at the anvil from one steel ingot; the helve hammer forges it as it forges a plate. A gear blank mold takes steel only.

Or smith one at the anvil from two steel ingots: put a second hot steel ingot on the work piece. The helve hammer forges it as it forges a plate, once both ingots are on. A large gear blank mold takes steel only.
